Recent conditions:
Regional weather records indicate that the orchard experienced a relatively dry winter and early spring, followed by a substantial rainfall during October. The dry lead-in is likely to have reduced stored soil moisture and increased reliance on irrigation, particularly within the sandy loam surface horizons and around trees with exposed roots or a restricted drip-irrigated wetted zone.
The heavy and repeated October rainfall subsequently replenished surface and subsoil moisture which promoted green orchard-floor growth and may have supported new root and vegetative flushing. At the time of inspection, the orchard appeared generally moisture-recharged in the topsoil rather than acutely drought-stressed.
The recent rainfall may temporarily mask limitations in the capacity or wetted area of the drip irrigation system.
Management history: Management history – Not assessed: Historical management practices, including pruning, fertiliser, irrigation, spray and soil-amendment programs, were outside the scope of this assessment and were not independently reviewed or verified. Findings are based on conditions observed at the time of inspection in field.
Inspection method and coverage: The inspection route and sampling locations were selected using Google Earth imagery to cover the principal orchard blocks, landscape positions and visible site variability. Sampling points were positioned to broadly align with an approximately 5 ha grid, while allowing practical adjustments for block boundaries, access and representative field conditions. The route was refined in the field to include representative trees and targeted trees showing atypical canopy or ground conditions. At six sites, we collected soil samples, examined soil profiles and root-zone conditions, and visually assessed canopy health and leaf vigour. Coverage comprised three blocks and numerous trees, with sampling locations recorded by GPS.
Inspection limitations:
The orchard is serviced by drip irrigation laterals. The water source, available storage, allocation, system capacity, operating pressure, emitter discharge and distribution uniformity were not independently reviewed.
Historical fertiliser applications were not reviewed, but nutritional status will be confirmed through representative soil analysis.
decision: The orchard presents a moderate agronomic concern and should be considered suitable for purchase only where the acquisition assessment includes appropriate technical verification and sufficient allowance for rehabilitation and capital works. The current rounded weighted condition is approximately 50%. Using 4.0 t/ha as a benchmark average crop, this condition indicates current average production potential of approximately 2.0 t/ha across the 31.18 ha bearing area.The principal material risks are widespread across Blocks 1–3 and align with recognised IOM red flags. The tall, upright and multi-leader canopy structure, including internal thinning and productive foliage concentrated around the canopy perimeter, aligns with the red flags height greater than row width and dead or unproductive centres. These conditions may reduce productive canopy volume, light penetration, spray coverage, harvest efficiency and future yield reliability. Corrective pruning and height reduction may also cause a temporary production penalty and may not restore a balanced canopy where structural decline is advanced. In these areas, staged redevelopment or tree replacement may be more economical than continued rehabilitation.The drip-irrigation system represents a further material uncertainty. The narrow-wetted area may not adequately service the mature root zone and could restrict feeder-root distribution and access to stored soil moisture. System capacity, pressure, distribution uniformity, emitter discharge and the depth and width of soil wetting were not independently verified. Remediation may require irrigation redesign, emitter replacement or conversion to under-tree micro-sprinklers. These works should be treated as potential purchaser-funded capital expenditure unless satisfactory system performance can be demonstrated.Widespread exposed roots, bare soil and areas of localised compaction align with the IOM red flags exposed roots and bare earth. These conditions provide an unsuitable environment for feeder-root development and may reduce water and nutrient uptake, increase susceptibility to Phytophthora and other pests and diseases, and contribute to reduced yield, poorer nut quality, canopy thinning, dead tops and progressive dieback. Rehabilitation should include restoring orchard-floor groundcover, applying suitable organic amendments or mulch, controlling erosion, alleviating compaction where practicable and maintaining favourable moisture conditions within the active feeder-root zone.The soil profiles were generally well to moderately well drained, with no widespread morphological evidence of prolonged waterlogging. A broad requirement for artificial subsurface drainage was not identified. Localised drainage, erosion, exposed-root and soil-surface constraints should nevertheless be managed to protect feeder roots and maintain a trafficable and harvestable orchard floor.If the recommended routine management actions are successfully implemented and the weighted condition improves to approximately 80%, average production potential may increase to approximately 3.2 t/ha. If the major capital works associated with canopy redevelopment and improved low risk AVG cultivars and higher kernel recovery, improved size and marketability, irrigation improvement and root-zone rehabilitation are fully funded and successfully implemented, a conditional weighted condition of approximately 100% would equate to a 4t/ha average production is achievable.These production figures are acquisition-screening scenarios rather than yield forecasts or guarantees. They assume a linear relationship between weighted condition and production and remain subject to seasonal conditions, cultivar performance, tree age, water availability, management execution and recovery time.Confidence in the assessment is moderate because it is based on a single inspection and limited historical records. The purchaser should obtain and review block-level yield and quality records, irrigation performance data, soil and leaf testing records, cultivar and tree-age information and historical management records. The acquisition assessment should also include a separately costed capital program and allowance for temporary production losses during rehabilitation.
risks: Representative trees across the inspected orchard displayed tall, strongly upright and multi-leader growth, extensive internal thinning, bare wood and productive foliage concentrated around the canopy perimeter. Crop load was generally average to low. The growth form is consistent with abnormal vertical growth characteristics. Cultivars are limited in yield expectations due AVG risk, nut size and quality and long-term yield.

The purchaser may inherit reduced productive canopy volume, inefficient spray coverage and elevated pruning costs. Corrective pruning and height reduction would cause a short-term production penalty and may not produce a balanced replacement canopy. Where the condition is widespread, staged block redevelopment may be more economical than rehabilitation and would require allowance for tree removal, irrigation modification, replanting and several years of foregone production. Evidence or acquisition condition: obtain cultivar and tree-age maps, at least five years of block-level yield and quality records, pruning and management history, and a costed comparison of canopy rehabilitation versus redevelopment.

The orchard is serviced by drip irrigation laterals. For mature trees, a narrow-wetted zone may restrict effective rooting volume and increase vulnerability to moisture stress, particularly within the sandy loam surface horizons.

The purchaser may inherit an irrigation system that does not uniformly meet mature-tree water demand or wet a sufficient proportion of the root zone. Remediation could require changes to irrigation scheduling, replacement or closer spacing of emitters, installation of additional drip laterals, or conversion to under-tree micro-sprinklers. These works may involve additional capital expenditure and temporary disruption to orchard operations. — Evidence or acquisition condition: Obtain irrigation design plans, water-source and allocation details, storage capacity, pump and filtration specifications, irrigation schedules and maintenance records. Commission a hydraulic performance assessment, including pressure and emitter-flow testing, distribution-uniformity calculation and soil-moisture or wetting-pattern assessment at multiple depths. Include an irrigation-upgrade allowance where system performance cannot be demonstrated.

The orchard exhibits widespread exposed roots and areas of bare and locally compacted soil. These conditions provide an unsuitable physical environment for feeder-root development by reducing surface protection, organic matter, soil moisture retention and aeration.

The purchaser may inherit a poorly functioning surface root zone with limited feeder-root development. Reduced feeder-root function may constrain water and nutrient uptake, increase susceptibility to Phytophthora and other pests and diseases, and contribute to reduced yield and nut quality, canopy thinning, dead tops and progressive dieback.Remediation may require restoring groundcover through soil profiling. Subsequently also by applying suitable organic amendments or mulch, controlling erosion, alleviating compaction where practicable, and adjusting irrigation to maintain favourable moisture conditions within the active feeder-root zone. Evidence of the condition and costed remediation allowances should be incorporated into the acquisition assessment.
